source.text: Συνίστημι δὲ ὑμῖν Φοίβην τὴν ἀδελφὴν ἡμῶν, οὖσαν καὶ διάκονον τῆς ἐκκλησίας τῆς ἐν Κεγχρεαῖς, ἵνα αὐτὴν προσδέξησθε ἐν κυρίῳ ἀξίως τῶν ἁγίων, καὶ παραστῆτε αὐτῇ ἐν ᾧ ἂν ὑμῶν χρῄζῃ πράγματι, καὶ γὰρ αὐτὴ προστάτις πολλῶν ἐγενήθη καὶ ἐμοῦ αὐτοῦ.

records.literal_gloss: I commend now to you Phoebe the sister of us, being also servant of the church the [one] in Cenchreae, \v 2 that her you may receive in [the] Lord worthily of the holy [ones], and may stand by her in whatever of you she may need matter, also for she patron of many became and of me myself.

en.L: Now I commend to you Phoebe our sister, who is also a deacon of the church in Cenchreae, \v 2 so that you may receive her in [the] Lord in a way worthy of the holy ones, and stand by her in whatever matter she may need from you, for she herself has also been a patron of many, and of me myself.
en.B: I commend to you our sister Phoebe, a deacon of the church in Cenchreae. \v 2 I ask you to welcome her in the Lord in the way God's holy people should, and to stand by her in anything she may need from you. She has been a patron to many, and to me as well.
en.R: I want to introduce our sister Phoebe to you. She is a deacon who serves the church in Cenchreae. \v 2 Please welcome her as one who belongs to the Lord, in the way God's people should welcome each other. Help her with anything she needs from you. She has used what she has to support and protect many people, and she has done that for me too.

decisions.choice: a letter of recommendation for Phoebe, who probably carried the letter
decisions.reason: "I commend" is the language of a letter of recommendation, which introduced a traveler to people who did not yet know her and asked them to receive her. Paul puts Phoebe first among all the names, and it is likely that she carried the letter to Rome, though the letter does not say so.

decisions.choice: Cenchreae, the eastern port of Corinth
decisions.reason: Cenchreae was a harbor town a few miles east of Corinth, on the Aegean side. Paul most likely wrote Romans from Corinth (see verse 23), so Phoebe belonged to a church near him.

decisions.choice: deacon: a recognized role of service in the church at Cenchreae
alternatives: servant: a general word for anyone who serves
decisions.reason: διάκονος means one who serves, and Paul uses it of himself, of Apollos and of Christ (15:8). Here it is tied to a particular church, "of the church in Cenchreae", which suggests a known role there, as in Philippians 1:1 and 1 Timothy 3:8-12, where the same word names an office. The word has the same form for a man or a woman. What a deacon did in a church this early is not known in detail; it may have included practical care, teaching or carrying messages. Others read the word here in its general sense: Phoebe served the church.

decisions.choice: receive her as believers should receive a fellow believer
alternatives: receive her as one worthy of the holy ones
decisions.reason: "In the Lord" means as a fellow member of the Lord's people, and "worthily of the holy ones" means in the way that befits God's people. The phrase is about how the readers welcome her, not about her worth.

decisions.choice: patron, benefactor: one who used her means and standing to support and protect others
decisions.reason: προστάτις is the feminine of a word for a protector or patron, someone of means who gave money, hospitality and legal or social protection to others. Paul says she has been this to many and to him. A related verb means "to lead" (12:8), so some read it as a position of leadership; but leading Paul himself is unlikely, and "helper" is too weak for a word used of patrons.

decisions.choice: the purpose clause becomes a request: I ask you to welcome her (B); Please welcome her (R)
alternatives: so that you may receive her
decisions.reason: In Greek the request hangs on "I commend" as its purpose. Balanced and Readable start a new sentence and make it a plain request, which is what the purpose clause asks for.

decisions.choice: the holy ones (L); God's holy people (B, R)
decisions.reason: As in 1:7 and Philippians 4:21: "saint" now usually means an exceptionally holy person, but Paul means every believer, set apart as God's own.

decisions.choice: She has used what she has to support and protect many people
decisions.reason: Readable explains "patron" (meaning decision m5), a word many young readers do not know.

source.text: Ἀσπάσασθε Πρίσκαν καὶ Ἀκύλαν τοὺς συνεργούς μου ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ, οἵτινες ὑπὲρ τῆς ψυχῆς μου τὸν ἑαυτῶν τράχηλον ὑπέθηκαν, οἷς οὐκ ἐγὼ μόνος εὐχαριστῶ ἀλλὰ καὶ πᾶσαι αἱ ἐκκλησίαι τῶν ἐθνῶν, καὶ τὴν κατ’ οἶκον αὐτῶν ἐκκλησίαν.

records.literal_gloss: Greet Prisca and Aquila the fellow workers of me in Christ Jesus, \v 4 who for the life of me the of themselves neck laid down, to whom not I alone give thanks but also all the churches of the Gentiles, \v 5 and the at house of them church.

en.L: Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} Jesus, \v 4 who laid down their own necks for my life, to whom not only I give thanks but also all the churches of the Gentiles; \v 5 and [greet] the church at their house.
en.B: Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus. \v 4 They put their own necks on the line for my life, and it is not only I who thank them: all the churches of the Gentiles do too. \v 5 Greet also the church that meets in their house.
en.R: Greet Prisca and Aquila. They have worked with me for {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus. \v 4 They risked their own lives to save mine. I am thankful to them, and so are all the churches among people who are not Jews. \v 5 Also greet the church that meets in their home.

decisions.choice: Prisca and Aquila, a Jewish couple who worked with Paul
decisions.reason: Acts calls her Priscilla, the familiar form of the name; Paul calls her Prisca (1 Corinthians 16:19, 2 Timothy 4:19). They left Rome when the emperor Claudius expelled the Jews, met Paul in Corinth and shared his trade of tentmaking, then worked with him in Ephesus (Acts 18:1-3, 18-26). Now they are back in Rome. Prisca is often named before her husband, which may mean she was the better known of the two.

decisions.choice: they risked their lives to save Paul
alternatives: they were literally threatened with execution
decisions.reason: "To lay down the neck" pictures offering one's neck to the sword: to risk death. When and where they did this is not said; it may have been in Ephesus, where Paul faced great danger (Acts 19:23-41, 1 Corinthians 15:32, 2 Corinthians 1:8-9).

decisions.choice: the Gentiles: the non-Jewish peoples
decisions.reason: Paul is the apostle to the Gentiles (11:13). The churches he founded among them owe their thanks to the couple who saved his life.

decisions.choice: a church that met in their house
decisions.reason: Early believers met in homes; there were no church buildings. "The church at their house" is the group of believers who met in Prisca and Aquila's home, as they had done in Ephesus (1 Corinthians 16:19). The names that follow in verses 10-15 may belong to other such groups in the city.

decisions.choice: Prisca
decisions.reason: Paul writes the shorter form of her name. The levels keep his form; Priscilla is the name Acts uses for the same woman (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus
decisions.reason: Title setting.

decisions.choice: [greet] (L); Greet also (B); Also greet (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek continues the list governed by "Greet" in verse 3; English needs the verb again after the long description in verse 4.

decisions.choice: people who are not Jews
decisions.reason: Readable says what "Gentiles" means, as in 1:16.

source.text: ἀσπάσασθε Ἐπαίνετον τὸν ἀγαπητόν μου, ὅς ἐστιν ἀπαρχὴ τῆς Ἀσίας εἰς Χριστόν.

records.literal_gloss: Greet Epaenetus the beloved of me, who is firstfruit of the Asia for Christ.

en.L: Greet Epaenetus my beloved, who is [the] firstfruits of Asia for {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}.
en.B: Greet my dear friend Epaenetus, the first of the harvest for {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} in Asia.
en.R: Greet Epaenetus, my dear friend. He was the first person in the province of Asia to become a follower of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.

decisions.choice: firstfruits: the first convert, the first of a harvest still to come
alternatives: the first portion offered to God
decisions.reason: ἀπαρχή is the first part of a harvest, which was given to God (Leviticus 23:10). Paul uses it of the first converts in a region (1 Corinthians 16:15). It says Epaenetus was the first, and it hints that many more would follow.

decisions.choice: Asia: the Roman province in the west of what is now Turkey
decisions.reason: Asia was a Roman province with Ephesus as its chief city. Paul worked there for more than two years (Acts 19:10).

decisions.choice: beloved: a dear friend in the faith
decisions.reason: ἀγαπητός is "loved", here a warm term for a fellow believer, as in verses 8, 9 and 12.

decisions.choice: dear friend
decisions.reason: "Beloved" is church language; "dear friend" says the same thing in everyday English.

decisions.choice: Epaenetus
decisions.reason: The standard English spelling of the name, which keeps the Greek diphthong.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}
decisions.reason: Title setting.

source.text: ἀσπάσασθε Μαριάμ, ἥτις πολλὰ ἐκοπίασεν εἰς ὑμᾶς.

records.literal_gloss: Greet Mary, who much labored for you.

en.L: Greet Mary, who labored much for you.
en.B: Greet Mary, who has worked hard for you.
en.R: Greet Mary. She has worked very hard for you.

decisions.choice: Mary, a believer in Rome
decisions.reason: The name is the Greek form of Miriam. Several women in the New Testament have it; nothing more is known of this Mary than what Paul says here.

decisions.choice: labored: hard work, here for the church
decisions.reason: κοπιάω means to work to the point of weariness. Paul uses it of his own work for the gospel and of others who work among believers (1 Corinthians 16:16, 1 Thessalonians 5:12).

decisions.choice: "for you"
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts read "for us", and a few "among you". "For you" means her work was for the church in Rome. The SBLGNT reads "for you". (From general knowledge of the manuscripts; to be checked against the apparatus.)

source.text: ἀσπάσασθε Ἀνδρόνικον καὶ Ἰουνίαν τοὺς συγγενεῖς μου καὶ συναιχμαλώτους μου, οἵτινές εἰσιν ἐπίσημοι ἐν τοῖς ἀποστόλοις, οἳ καὶ πρὸ ἐμοῦ γέγοναν ἐν Χριστῷ.

records.literal_gloss: Greet Andronicus and Junia the kinsfolk of me and fellow prisoners of me, who are notable among the apostles, who also before me have been in Christ.

en.L: Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kinsfolk and my fellow prisoners, who are notable among the apostles, who also were in {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} before me.
en.B: Greet Andronicus and Junia, my fellow Jews, who were in prison with me. They are prominent among the apostles, and they were in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} earlier than I was.
en.R: Greet Andronicus and Junia. They are Jews like me, and they were in prison with me. They stand out among the apostles. They belonged to {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} even before I did.

decisions.choice: Junia, a woman
decisions.reason: The earliest manuscripts were written without accents, so Ἰουνίαν could be read as the woman's name Junia or as a man's name Junias. Junia was a common Latin name for women; a man's name Junias has not been found anywhere else. Early Christian writers who comment on the verse took Junia as a woman, and the SBLGNT accents the word as a woman's name. A few manuscripts have Julia, the name in verse 15. Andronicus and Junia were probably a married couple, like Prisca and Aquila. (From general knowledge of the manuscripts; to be checked against the apparatus.)

decisions.choice: kinsfolk: fellow Jews
decisions.reason: συγγενής can mean a relative, but Paul uses it for his fellow Israelites in 9:3, and he gives it to six people in this chapter (verses 7, 11, 21). They are most likely Jews like him rather than members of his family.

decisions.choice: fellow prisoners: they had been in prison with Paul
decisions.reason: The word is literally "fellow captives". Paul was imprisoned many times (2 Corinthians 11:23); where these two shared a prison with him is not known.

decisions.choice: prominent among the apostles: they were themselves counted as apostles
alternatives: well known to the apostles: respected by the apostles, but not apostles themselves
decisions.reason: "Among" with a group of people usually places someone inside the group, so the phrase most naturally means that they were outstanding apostles. "Apostle" here would have the wider sense of a messenger sent out to plant churches, as with Barnabas (Acts 14:14) and the messengers of the churches (2 Corinthians 8:23), not one of the Twelve. Others read it as "well known to the apostles", since the word for "notable" can be followed by the people to whom someone is known. Both readings are possible Greek.

decisions.choice: they became believers before Paul did
decisions.reason: "Were in Christ before me" means they belonged to Christ before Paul's own conversion, so they were among the earliest believers, perhaps from Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: kinsfolk (L); fellow Jews (B); Jews like me (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the word that covers both family and people; Balanced and Readable say which is meant (meaning decision m2). "Countrymen" would leave out Junia.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}
decisions.reason: Title setting.

source.text: ἀσπάσασθε Ἀμπλιᾶτον τὸν ἀγαπητόν μου ἐν κυρίῳ.

records.literal_gloss: Greet Ampliatus the beloved of me in [the] Lord.

en.L: Greet Ampliatus, my beloved in [the] Lord.
en.B: Greet Ampliatus, whom I love in the Lord.
en.R: Greet Ampliatus. He is my dear friend, and we both belong to the Lord.

decisions.choice: Ampliatus: a Latin name
decisions.reason: Ampliatus was a common Latin name in Rome, often borne by slaves and freed slaves. Many of the names in this list are of that kind, which shows the church included people of low social standing.

decisions.choice: love grounded in their shared belonging to the Lord
decisions.reason: "In the Lord" says what binds Paul and Ampliatus together: they both belong to the Lord Jesus.

decisions.choice: and we both belong to the Lord
decisions.reason: Readable spells out what "in the Lord" means here (meaning decision m2).

source.text: ἀσπάσασθε Οὐρβανὸν τὸν συνεργὸν ἡμῶν ἐν Χριστῷ καὶ Στάχυν τὸν ἀγαπητόν μου.

records.literal_gloss: Greet Urbanus the fellow worker of us in Christ and Stachys the beloved of me.

en.L: Greet Urbanus, our fellow worker in {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, and Stachys my beloved.
en.B: Greet Urbanus, our co-worker in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, and my dear friend Stachys.
en.R: Greet Urbanus, who works with us for {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}. And greet my dear friend Stachys.

decisions.choice: our fellow worker: he worked with Paul and his companions
decisions.reason: Paul says "our" here, not "my" as with Prisca and Aquila in verse 3. Urbanus had worked with Paul's wider circle, or with the church generally.

decisions.choice: Urbanus and Stachys: a Latin and a Greek name
decisions.reason: Urbanus is a Latin name ("of the city"), Stachys a Greek one ("ear of grain"). Nothing more is known of either.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}
decisions.reason: Title setting.

decisions.choice: dear friend
decisions.reason: As in verse 5.

source.text: ἀσπάσασθε Ἀπελλῆν τὸν δόκιμον ἐν Χριστῷ.

records.literal_gloss: Greet Apelles the approved [one] in Christ.

en.L: Greet Apelles, the approved [one] in {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}.
en.B: Greet Apelles, who has been tested and found true in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.
en.R: Greet Apelles. He has been tested, and he has proved faithful to {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.

decisions.choice: approved: tested and proven genuine
decisions.reason: δόκιμος describes metal or coins that have been tested and found genuine. Paul uses the related noun for character proved under trial (5:4). Apelles had come through some test of his faith.

decisions.choice: approved as one who belongs to Christ
decisions.reason: "In Christ" places his tested character within his life as a believer.

decisions.choice: tested and found true (B); tested ... proved faithful (R)
decisions.reason: "Approved" alone could sound like a formal permission. Balanced and Readable say what the word pictures: proved genuine under testing.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}
decisions.reason: Title setting.

source.text: ἀσπάσασθε τοὺς ἐκ τῶν Ἀριστοβούλου.

records.literal_gloss: Greet those from the [ones] of Aristobulus.

en.L: Greet those from the [household] of Aristobulus.
en.B: Greet those who belong to the household of Aristobulus.
en.R: Greet the people of Aristobulus's household.

decisions.choice: the members of Aristobulus's household
decisions.reason: The Greek says only "those from the [people] of Aristobulus". In a Roman household this means mainly the slaves and freed slaves who belonged to it. Aristobulus himself is not greeted, so he may not have been a believer, or may have died.

decisions.choice: Aristobulus: perhaps a member of Herod's family living in Rome
decisions.reason: A grandson of Herod the Great named Aristobulus lived in Rome and was a friend of the emperor Claudius. If this is his household, its servants may have passed to the emperor's household after his death and kept his name. The identification is possible but cannot be proved.

decisions.choice: [household] (L); household (B, R)
decisions.reason: The Greek leaves the noun out; "household" is what the phrase means (meaning decision m1).

source.text: ἀσπάσασθε Ἡρῳδίωνα τὸν συγγενῆ μου.

records.literal_gloss: Greet Herodion the kinsman of me.

en.L: Greet Herodion, my kinsman.
en.B: Greet Herodion, my fellow Jew.
en.R: Greet Herodion, who is a Jew like me.

decisions.choice: kinsman: a fellow Jew
decisions.reason: συγγενής is used for fellow Israelites in 9:3. As with Andronicus and Junia (verse 7), it most likely means a fellow Jew rather than a member of Paul's family.

decisions.choice: Herodion: a name that suggests a link with Herod's family
decisions.reason: The name comes from Herod. Herodion may have been a slave or freed slave of Herod's family, which would fit a Jew placed next to the household of Aristobulus. This is a guess from the name.

decisions.choice: fellow Jew (B); a Jew like me (R)
decisions.reason: As in verse 7.

source.text: ἀσπάσασθε τοὺς ἐκ τῶν Ναρκίσσου τοὺς ὄντας ἐν κυρίῳ.

records.literal_gloss: Greet those from the [ones] of Narcissus, the [ones] being in [the] Lord.

en.L: Greet those from the [household] of Narcissus who are in [the] Lord.
en.B: Greet those in the household of Narcissus who belong to the Lord.
en.R: Greet the people in the household of Narcissus who belong to the Lord.

decisions.choice: only the believers in that household
decisions.reason: "Who are in the Lord" limits the greeting: not everyone in the household was a believer.

decisions.choice: Narcissus: perhaps the powerful freed slave of the emperor Claudius
decisions.reason: A freed slave named Narcissus was one of Claudius's most powerful officials and died in AD 54, a few years before Paul wrote. His slaves would then have passed to the emperor's household while still known by his name. The name was common, so this cannot be proved.

decisions.choice: [household] (L); household (B, R)
decisions.reason: As in verse 10.

source.text: ἀσπάσασθε Τρύφαιναν καὶ Τρυφῶσαν τὰς κοπιώσας ἐν κυρίῳ.

records.literal_gloss: Greet Tryphaena and Tryphosa the [ones] laboring in [the] Lord.

en.L: Greet Tryphaena and Tryphosa, who labor in [the] Lord.
en.B: Greet Tryphaena and Tryphosa, women who work hard in the Lord.
en.R: Greet Tryphaena and Tryphosa. They work hard for the Lord.

decisions.choice: two women, perhaps sisters
decisions.reason: The two names come from the same root and sound alike, which suggests sisters, perhaps twins. The Greek participle that describes them is feminine.

decisions.choice: laboring: working hard for the church
decisions.reason: The same verb as in verse 6: work to the point of weariness, here "in the Lord", work done as his servants.

decisions.choice: for the Lord
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly that the work is done for the Lord.

source.text: ἀσπάσασθε Περσίδα τὴν ἀγαπητήν, ἥτις πολλὰ ἐκοπίασεν ἐν κυρίῳ.

records.literal_gloss: Greet Persis the beloved, who much labored in [the] Lord.

en.L: Greet Persis the beloved, who labored much in [the] Lord.
en.B: Greet dear Persis, who has worked hard in the Lord.
en.R: Greet our dear friend Persis. She has worked very hard for the Lord.

decisions.choice: the beloved: dear to the whole church
decisions.reason: With the men in verses 5, 8 and 9 Paul writes "my beloved"; here he writes "the beloved", dear to all the believers.

decisions.choice: she labored: her work in the past
decisions.reason: Paul uses the past tense for Persis where he used the present for Tryphaena and Tryphosa. Her hard work may have been earlier; the text does not say why.

decisions.choice: our dear friend
decisions.reason: Readable says "our", for the shared affection the article implies (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: for the Lord
decisions.reason: As in 12a.

source.text: ἀσπάσασθε Ῥοῦφον τὸν ἐκλεκτὸν ἐν κυρίῳ καὶ τὴν μητέρα αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐμοῦ.

records.literal_gloss: Greet Rufus the chosen [one] in [the] Lord, and the mother of him and of me.

en.L: Greet Rufus, the chosen [one] in [the] Lord, and his mother and mine.
en.B: Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and greet his mother, who has also been a mother to me.
en.R: Greet Rufus, whom the Lord has chosen. Greet his mother too. She has been like a mother to me.

decisions.choice: chosen in the Lord
decisions.reason: ἐκλεκτός means chosen, and in Paul it describes all believers as chosen by God (8:33). Said of one man, it may stress that he is an outstanding believer, a "choice" man. The levels keep "chosen".

decisions.choice: his mother, who has also mothered Paul
decisions.reason: "His mother and mine" means she had cared for Paul as if he were her own son, not that Paul and Rufus were brothers.

decisions.choice: Rufus: perhaps the son of Simon of Cyrene
decisions.reason: Mark 15:21 names Simon of Cyrene, who carried Jesus' cross, as "the father of Alexander and Rufus", as if the readers knew them. If Mark wrote for believers in Rome, this may be the same Rufus. The name was common, so this is uncertain.

decisions.choice: who has also been a mother to me (B); She has been like a mother to me (R)
decisions.reason: Spelled out so the phrase is not read as Paul's own mother (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: whom the Lord has chosen
decisions.reason: Readable makes the Lord the one who chose. In Paul God chooses (8:33), and Rufus belongs to the Lord; the sense is the same.

source.text: ἀσπάσασθε Ἀσύγκριτον, Φλέγοντα, Ἑρμῆν, Πατροβᾶν, Ἑρμᾶν καὶ τοὺς σὺν αὐτοῖς ἀδελφούς.

records.literal_gloss: Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the with them brothers.

en.L: Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}} with them.
en.B: Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}} who are with them.
en.R: Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, and Hermas. Also greet the {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}} who meet with them.

decisions.choice: a group of believers, perhaps a house church
decisions.reason: Five men are named together with "the brothers with them", which suggests a group that met together, perhaps in one house or among the workers of one household. Several of the names were common among slaves and freed slaves.

decisions.choice: fellow believers, men and women
decisions.reason: ἀδελφός is Paul's usual word for fellow members of the church, including the women among them, as in 1:13.

decisions.choice: {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}
decisions.reason: No particular men are meant, so the inclusive default applies.

decisions.choice: who meet with them
decisions.reason: Readable says how they were "with them": as a group that met together (meaning decision m1).

source.text: ἀσπάσασθε Φιλόλογον καὶ Ἰουλίαν, Νηρέα καὶ τὴν ἀδελφὴν αὐτοῦ, καὶ Ὀλυμπᾶν καὶ τοὺς σὺν αὐτοῖς πάντας ἁγίους.

records.literal_gloss: Greet Philologus and Julia, Nereus and the sister of him, and Olympas, and the with them all holy [ones].

en.L: Greet Philologus and Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas, and all the holy ones with them.
en.B: Greet Philologus and Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas, and all God's holy people who are with them.
en.R: Greet Philologus and Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas. Also greet all of God's people who are with them.

decisions.choice: another group of believers, perhaps a family
decisions.reason: Philologus and Julia are named as a pair, probably husband and wife or brother and sister; Nereus and his sister may have been their children. With "all the holy ones with them" they seem to be another group that met together.

decisions.choice: holy ones: believers
decisions.reason: As in verse 2 and 1:7: all believers, set apart as God's own.

decisions.choice: holy ones (L); God's holy people (B); God's people (R)
decisions.reason: As in verse 2.

source.text: Ἀσπάσασθε ἀλλήλους ἐν φιλήματι ἁγίῳ.

records.literal_gloss: Greet one another with a kiss holy.

en.L: Greet one another with a holy kiss.
en.B: Greet one another with a holy kiss.
en.R: Greet each other with a holy kiss.

decisions.choice: the kiss of greeting among believers
decisions.reason: A kiss was a common greeting among family and close friends. Paul calls it holy: the greeting of people who are now one family in God. He asks for it in other letters too (1 Corinthians 16:20, 2 Corinthians 13:12, 1 Thessalonians 5:26).

source.text: Ἀσπάζονται ὑμᾶς αἱ ἐκκλησίαι πᾶσαι τοῦ Χριστοῦ.

records.literal_gloss: Greet you the churches all of the Christ.

en.L: All the churches of the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} greet you.
en.B: All the churches of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} send you greetings.
en.R: All the churches of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} send you their greetings.

decisions.choice: all the churches Paul has worked among
decisions.reason: Paul speaks for the churches he knows, perhaps especially those whose messengers were with him to take the collection to Jerusalem (15:25-26, Acts 20:4). "Churches of Christ" is found only here in Paul's letters; he usually says "churches of God".

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}
decisions.reason: Title setting.

source.text: Παρακαλῶ δὲ ὑμᾶς, ἀδελφοί, σκοπεῖν τοὺς τὰς διχοστασίας καὶ τὰ σκάνδαλα παρὰ τὴν διδαχὴν ἣν ὑμεῖς ἐμάθετε ποιοῦντας, καὶ ἐκκλίνετε ἀπ’ αὐτῶν·

records.literal_gloss: I urge now you, brothers, to watch the [ones] the divisions and the stumbling blocks contrary to the teaching which you learned causing, and turn away from them;

en.L: Now I urge you, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, to watch out for those who cause the divisions and the stumbling blocks contrary to the teaching that you learned, and turn away from them;
en.B: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, I urge you to keep an eye on those who stir up divisions and put stumbling blocks in people's way, against the teaching you were taught. Keep away from them.
en.R: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, I beg you to watch out for people who split the church apart. They make others trip up and fall away from the teaching you learned. Stay away from them.

decisions.choice: stumbling blocks: things that make believers fall away
decisions.reason: σκάνδαλον is a trap or obstacle that trips someone up. Paul used it in 14:13 of anything that causes a fellow believer to fall. Here it means teaching and conduct that lead believers away from the faith.

decisions.choice: the teaching the Roman believers had already received
decisions.reason: "The teaching that you learned" is the pattern of teaching they were handed when they believed (6:17). The trouble-makers go against it.

decisions.choice: a warning against people who are not named
decisions.reason: Paul does not say who these people are, and the warning comes suddenly at the end of the letter. Verse 18 describes them as serving their own appetites and using smooth talk, as Philippians 3:18-19 describes enemies of the cross. They may not yet have reached Rome.

decisions.choice: fellow believers, men and women
decisions.reason: As in verse 14.

decisions.choice: {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}
decisions.reason: Paul addresses the whole church.

decisions.choice: Keep away from them / Stay away from them, as a new sentence
decisions.reason: The Greek joins the second command with "and". Balanced and Readable give it a sentence of its own so it is heard as a command.

decisions.choice: split the church apart
decisions.reason: Readable says what divisions do to a church.

source.text: οἱ γὰρ τοιοῦτοι τῷ κυρίῳ ἡμῶν Χριστῷ οὐ δουλεύουσιν ἀλλὰ τῇ ἑαυτῶν κοιλίᾳ, καὶ διὰ τῆς χρηστολογίας καὶ εὐλογίας ἐξαπατῶσι τὰς καρδίας τῶν ἀκάκων.

records.literal_gloss: The for such [ones] the Lord of us Christ not serve but the of themselves belly, and through the smooth talk and flattery they deceive the hearts of the innocent.

en.L: For such [people] do not serve our Lord {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} but their own belly, and by smooth talk and fine words they deceive the hearts of the unsuspecting.
en.B: People like this are not serving our Lord {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}; they are serving their own stomachs. With smooth talk and fine-sounding words they lead astray the hearts of trusting people.
en.R: People like that are not serving our Lord {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}. They serve their own appetites. They use smooth talk and flattering words to fool people who do not suspect anything.

decisions.choice: their own belly: their own appetites and desires
decisions.reason: To serve the belly is to live for one's own desires and gain, as Paul says of the enemies of the cross in Philippians 3:19. Some think of quarrels over food (chapter 14), but the phrase is a common picture of self-indulgence.

decisions.choice: smooth talk and fine words: speech that charms and flatters
decisions.reason: χρηστολογία is plausible, pleasant talk; εὐλογία usually means "blessing" or "praise", and here fine-sounding words that flatter. Paul may be playing on the word: their "blessings" deceive.

decisions.choice: the unsuspecting: people without guile, who do not expect deceit
decisions.reason: ἄκακος means without evil, not suspecting evil in others. It is not a word of blame; such people are easily deceived because they are honest themselves.

decisions.choice: serve as slaves
decisions.reason: δουλεύω is the verb related to the noun for "slave": to serve as one who belongs to a master. They are slaves of their appetites, not of Christ.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}
decisions.reason: Title setting.

decisions.choice: stomachs (B); appetites (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the picture in a modern word; Readable says what it means (meaning decision m1).

source.text: ἡ γὰρ ὑμῶν ὑπακοὴ εἰς πάντας ἀφίκετο· ἐφ’ ὑμῖν οὖν χαίρω, θέλω δὲ ὑμᾶς σοφοὺς εἶναι εἰς τὸ ἀγαθόν, ἀκεραίους δὲ εἰς τὸ κακόν.

records.literal_gloss: The for of you obedience to all [people] reached; over you therefore I rejoice, I want but you wise to be toward the good, innocent but toward the evil.

en.L: For your obedience has reached all [people]; therefore I rejoice over you, but I want you to be wise toward what is good, and innocent toward what is evil.
en.B: Everyone has heard of your obedience, and so I am glad about you. Still, I want you to be wise in what is good and to keep yourselves untouched by what is evil.
en.R: Everyone has heard how you obey God, and that makes me very happy about you. But I want you to be wise about doing good, and to stay pure and have nothing to do with evil.

decisions.choice: for: the reason for the warning
decisions.reason: Paul gives the reason he can warn them: their obedience is known everywhere, so he trusts them, but their good name also makes them a target for such teachers.

decisions.choice: obedience: their response of faith to the gospel
decisions.reason: In 1:5 and 1:8 Paul speaks of "the obedience of faith" and of their faith being known in the whole world. Their obedience is their faith lived out.

decisions.choice: innocent: unmixed, pure, untouched by evil
decisions.reason: ἀκέραιος describes something unmixed, like wine without water or metal without alloy. Jesus uses it of doves (Matthew 10:16). Paul wants them to know good well and to have no share in evil.

decisions.choice: how you obey God
decisions.reason: Readable names God as the one they obey.

decisions.choice: keep yourselves untouched by what is evil (B); stay pure and have nothing to do with evil (R)
decisions.reason: "Innocent toward evil" is unclear in English; Balanced and Readable say what the word means (meaning decision m3).

source.text: ὁ δὲ θεὸς τῆς εἰρήνης συντρίψει τὸν Σατανᾶν ὑπὸ τοὺς πόδας ὑμῶν ἐν τάχει.

records.literal_gloss: The and God of the peace will crush the Satan under the feet of you in quickness.

en.L: And the God of peace will crush Satan under your feet in a short time.
en.B: And before long the God of peace will crush Satan under your feet.
en.R: God, who gives peace, will soon crush Satan under your feet.

decisions.choice: an echo of Genesis 3:15
decisions.reason: God told the serpent that the woman's offspring would crush its head (Genesis 3:15). Paul's promise echoes it: God will defeat Satan, and his people will share the victory.

decisions.choice: the God of peace: the God who gives peace and makes it
decisions.reason: Paul used the title in 15:33. Here it stands against the people who cause divisions (verse 17): God himself brings peace and will defeat the one behind the trouble.

decisions.choice: soon
decisions.reason: The phrase can mean "quickly" or "soon". With a future verb it most likely says the victory will not be long in coming.

decisions.choice: Satan: the adversary
decisions.reason: Satan is a Hebrew word for "adversary", the name of the enemy of God and his people.

decisions.choice: God, who gives peace
decisions.reason: Readable says what "God of peace" means (meaning decision m2) and keeps the word "peace".

source.text: ἡ χάρις τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ μεθ’ ὑμῶν.

records.literal_gloss: The grace of the Lord of us Jesus Christ with you.

en.L: The grace of our Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} [be] with you.
en.B: May the grace of our Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} be with you.
en.R: May the grace of our Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} be with you.

decisions.choice: the blessing stands here, with "Christ"
alternatives: the blessing left out here and placed after verse 23
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts have "our Lord Jesus" without "Christ"; the pinned SBLGNT data has "Christ" and marks the word as uncertain. Some Greek-Latin manuscripts leave this blessing out here and give it after verse 23 instead (verse 24). (From general knowledge of the manuscripts; to be checked against the apparatus.)

decisions.choice: a prayer: may grace be with you
decisions.reason: There is no verb. As in the closing of his other letters, it is a blessing prayed over the readers.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}
decisions.reason: Title setting.

source.text: Ἀσπάζεται ὑμᾶς Τιμόθεος ὁ συνεργός μου, καὶ Λούκιος καὶ Ἰάσων καὶ Σωσίπατρος οἱ συγγενεῖς μου.

records.literal_gloss: Greets you Timothy the fellow worker of me, and Lucius and Jason and Sosipater the kinsfolk of me.

en.L: Timothy my fellow worker greets you, and Lucius and Jason and Sosipater my kinsfolk.
en.B: Timothy, my co-worker, sends you greetings, and so do Lucius, Jason, and Sosipater, my fellow Jews.
en.R: Timothy, who works with me, sends you greetings. So do Lucius, Jason, and Sosipater, who are Jews like me.

decisions.choice: Timothy, Paul's closest co-worker
decisions.reason: Timothy joined Paul in Lystra (Acts 16:1-3) and worked with him for many years (Philippians 2:19-22). He was with Paul in Corinth when Romans was written.

decisions.choice: Lucius, Jason and Sosipater: Jewish believers with Paul
decisions.reason: A Jason received Paul in Thessalonica (Acts 17:5-9), and a Sopater of Berea, a short form of Sosipater, travelled with Paul when he left Greece (Acts 20:4). A Lucius of Cyrene is named in Acts 13:1. These may be the same men, but the names were common.

decisions.choice: kinsfolk: fellow Jews
decisions.reason: As in verses 7 and 11.

decisions.choice: fellow Jews (B); Jews like me (R)
decisions.reason: As in verse 7.

source.text: ἀσπάζομαι ὑμᾶς ἐγὼ Τέρτιος ὁ γράψας τὴν ἐπιστολὴν ἐν κυρίῳ.

records.literal_gloss: Greet you I Tertius the [one] having written the letter in [the] Lord.

en.L: I, Tertius, who wrote the letter, greet you in [the] Lord.
en.B: I, Tertius, the one who wrote this letter down, greet you in the Lord.
en.R: I am Tertius. I wrote down this letter for Paul, and I send you greetings as one who belongs to the Lord.

decisions.choice: Tertius, the scribe who wrote the letter as Paul spoke it
decisions.reason: Letters were often written by a trained scribe as the author dictated. Paul used scribes for other letters too and sometimes added a line in his own hand (1 Corinthians 16:21, Galatians 6:11). Here the scribe adds his own greeting.

decisions.choice: "in the Lord" goes with "greet"
decisions.reason: Tertius greets them as a fellow believer, as Paul asks the Romans to receive Phoebe "in the Lord" (verse 2). The phrase could also say that he wrote the letter as a service to the Lord.

decisions.choice: for Paul
decisions.reason: Readable says for whom Tertius wrote, since the letter is Paul's (meaning decision m1).

source.text: ἀσπάζεται ὑμᾶς Γάϊος ὁ ξένος μου καὶ ὅλης τῆς ἐκκλησίας.

records.literal_gloss: Greets you Gaius the host of me and of whole the church.

en.L: Gaius, host of me and of the whole church, greets you.
en.B: Gaius, who is host to me and to the whole church, sends you greetings.
en.R: Gaius sends you greetings. I am staying in his home, and he welcomes the whole church there.

decisions.choice: Gaius, a believer in Corinth
decisions.reason: Paul baptized a Gaius in Corinth (1 Corinthians 1:14). Paul was probably staying with him in Corinth while writing this letter.

decisions.choice: host: he gives hospitality to Paul and to the whole church
alternatives: host of the whole church meeting in his house
host to all believers who pass through
decisions.reason: ξένος usually means a stranger or guest; here, as sometimes elsewhere, it means the host who receives guests. "Of the whole church" may mean the church in Corinth met in his house, or that he welcomed any believer who came.

decisions.choice: I am staying in his home, and he welcomes the whole church there
alternatives: my host and the host of the whole church
decisions.reason: Readable explains "host" and follows the reading that the church met in his house.

source.text: ἀσπάζεται ὑμᾶς Ἔραστος ὁ οἰκονόμος τῆς πόλεως καὶ Κούαρτος ὁ ἀδελφός.

records.literal_gloss: Greets you Erastus the steward of the city and Quartus the brother.

en.L: Erastus the steward of the city greets you, and Quartus the brother.
en.B: Erastus, the city treasurer, sends you greetings, and so does our brother Quartus.
en.R: Erastus, who looks after the city's money, sends you greetings. So does our brother Quartus.

decisions.choice: the city treasurer, a public official of Corinth
alternatives: the manager of the city's property
decisions.reason: οἰκονόμος is a manager or steward. "Of the city" makes Erastus a city official, most likely in charge of its finances. An inscription found in Corinth names an Erastus who paved a square at his own expense while holding public office; he may be the same man.

decisions.choice: the brother: a fellow believer
decisions.reason: "The brother" names Quartus as a fellow believer, as Paul calls Timothy and others "the brother" (2 Corinthians 1:1).

decisions.choice: our brother
decisions.reason: English says "our brother" for a fellow believer (meaning decision m2).

source.text: Ἡ χάρις τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν. Ἀμήν.

records.literal_gloss: The grace of the Lord of us Jesus Christ with all of you. Amen.

en.L: The grace of our Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} [be] with all of you. Amen.
en.B: May the grace of our Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} be with all of you. Amen.
en.R: May the grace of our Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} be with all of you. Amen.

decisions.choice: one record: the blessing and its Amen
decisions.reason: The source text puts a full stop before "Amen". The one word is the response to the blessing and cannot stand as a sentence of its own, so the two are kept together.

decisions.choice: verse 24 is kept as the pinned source text has it
alternatives: verse 24 left out, with the blessing only at verse 20
the doxology traditionally numbered 16:25-27 added here
decisions.reason: Manuscripts end Romans in different ways. Many later manuscripts repeat the blessing of verse 20 here as verse 24; the oldest leave it out. The doxology (the closing praise to God traditionally numbered 16:25-27) stands after 16:23 in the oldest manuscripts, after 14:23 in many later ones, after 15:33 in the oldest papyrus, in two places in some, and is missing in a few. The SBLGNT data this project pins prints verse 24, marked as a place where manuscripts differ, and has no 16:25-27. Reviewers must check against the printed SBLGNT and its apparatus whether verse 24 belongs in the text and whether the doxology must be added as a record of its own. (From general knowledge of the manuscripts.)

decisions.choice: "Amen" stands
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts that have the blessing lack "Amen"; the pinned text marks the word as uncertain. (To be checked against the apparatus.)

decisions.choice: a prayer: may grace be with all of you
decisions.reason: As in verse 20, there is no verb: a blessing over all the readers.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}
decisions.reason: Title setting.
